description:
Hi, I’m Daniel, a member of Albania’s national robotics team. I do competitive programming (Java, C++, Python) and have built Flutter apps, a robot simulator and a bionic arm. I cover coding, algorithms and hardware, and I finish what I start with a polished result.

Looking for:

A data science/astronomy person to read NASA datasets and keep our approach scientifically sound

A strong presenter to lead the pitch and video
summary: Narthecium is a health monitoring tool for crews far from Earth. It learns each astronaut’s own baseline and uses change detection to catch slow drift in sleep, mood, heart rate, radiation dose and cabin air. It covers all five NASA spaceflight hazards with color-coded rings, then attributes drift to the cabin or the person by comparing crewmates and habitat sensors. Its Machine Spirit Twin shows two bodies side by side, one following countermeasures and one neglecting them, so the consequences are visible. Rule-based alerts decide escalation, and an explainer only rewords them. It keeps working during Mars communication delays and builds a one-page report for flight surgeons.
details:
• Functionality: A simulated 180-day mission produces health and habitat data. A drift engine (CUSUM on personal baselines) drives five hazard rings, a four-level escalation ladder, protocol cards and cause attribution. A clickable body model explains why each organ system is monitored. The Twin projects the effect of countermeasures. A ground report summarizes the state.
  • Benefits: Astronauts get early, understandable warnings and know what to do while waiting for Earth.
  • Impact: It supports autonomy on Moon and Mars missions with communication delay.
  • Technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, Google Fonts (Cinzel, Chakra Petch), and a seeded random simulator.
  • Creativity: Personal-baseline drift, cabin-versus-person attribution, the Twin, and peer observation.
  • Factors considered: The five hazards, safety, a rules-over-AI split, accessibility and communication delay. Projection numbers are illustrative and labeled that way. Simulated data limits reliability.
projectRefs: CSA, Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
